What happens when cuttings settle in the bore?
On every drill, cuttings are falling back into the hole as fast as you're making them. Your fluid's job is to lift them clear, all the way to surface, without a break in the annulus.

Slow that fluid down, or lose your suspension properties, and cuttings drop out. They don't just sit there, they build a bed along the low side of the hole, cutting your effective annulus and shoving up torque and drag.

Leave that bed in place and the bore wall starts working against you. Loose material shifts, the hole loses support, and you're looking at pack-off or a collapse before you know it.

Clean hole is stable hole. It comes down to keeping enough fluid velocity and suspension to carry cuttings out, not just push mud around.
What ground conditions have given your crew the most trouble keeping the bore clean?

Keep the hole clean, keep the job running.
Tricky ground doesn't forgive a fluid that can't carry its load. That's the gap Carry Flow is built to close.

It holds cuttings in suspension and keeps them moving through the annulus, so you're not fighting the bed-up and torque spikes we talked about on Wednesday. Less settling means less drag on the string and less risk to hole integrity.

On a critical bore, that's not a nice-to-have, it's what keeps you drilling instead of tripping out to deal with a pack-off.

If suspension is where your fluid program is getting tested, that's exactly where Carry Flow is built to hold up.
When's the last time your fluid program was the thing that saved a critical bore?
